# CI review

## Slido question:

Which of the following represents the definition of a confidence interval?

![](/assets/slido-which-of-the-following-represents-the-ci.png)


## Terms

::: card-list
- $\mu$ is the true mean
- $x$ is the result from a single participant
- $\bar{x}$ is the mean from *any* experiment
- $\bar{x}_{observed}$ is the mean that we observe from *our* particular experiment
- The mean of the means (aka the mean of $\bar{x}$) is so close to $\mu$ that we assume they are equivalent.
    - mean of $\bar{x} = \mu$

:::

---

```{r}


library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

area_between_norm <- function(mu, sd, alpha, minlab, meanlab, maxlab, xaxis, title){
percent <- paste0(as.character((1-alpha)*100),"%")

x <- seq(mu - 4*sd, mu + 4*sd, length.out = 1000)

df <- tibble(
  x = x,
  y = dnorm(x, mu, sd)
)

lower <- qnorm(alpha/2, mu, sd)
upper <- qnorm(1-(alpha/2), mu, sd)

mid_x <- (lower + upper) / 2
mid_y <- dnorm(mid_x, mu, sd) * 0.5

ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_area(
    aes(y = ifelse(x > lower & x < upper, y, 0)),
    alpha = 0.2,
    fill="steelblue"
  ) +
    labs(x = xaxis, title = title) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lower, mu, upper), linetype = "dashed") + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-5,5), breaks = c(lower, mu, upper), labels = c(minlab,meanlab,maxlab)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 10) + 
   theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1), face = "bold",
        hjust = 0.5,margin = margin(b = rel(4))),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5),
    axis.ticks.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.8),
    axis.ticks.length.x = unit(4, "pt"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(2), margin = margin(t = rel(4))),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = rel(1.5), face = "bold", margin = margin(t = rel(3))),
    plot.margin = margin(b = rel(2), r = rel(2), l=rel(2), t=rel(2)),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
  plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "transparent")) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = mid_x,
    y = mid_y,
    label = percent,
    size = 8
  )
}


plot1 <- area_between_norm(mu=0, sd=2, alpha=0.05, minlab="a", meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab="b", xaxis=expression(bar(x) ~ "(means from experiments)"), title="1. Sampling distribution")

plot2 <- area_between_norm(mu=0, sd=1, alpha=0.05, minlab="-1.96", meanlab="0", maxlab="1.96", xaxis=expression(Z == frac(bar(x) - mu, SE)), title=paste0("2. Normalize dist. Z ~ Norm(0,1)"))

plot3 <- area_between_norm(mu=0, sd=2, alpha=0.05, minlab=expression(mu-1.96 %*% SE), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(mu+1.96 %*% SE), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title=paste0("3. Substitute from Z to get a and b"))

plot1+plot2+plot3+theme(plot.margin = margin(b = 10, r = 10, l=10, t=10),)

```

#3 is what we would *like* to know.

**Problem: we don't know the true mean, $\mu$**

```{r}
#| fig-height: 6

plot3
```

::::


:::: column


From here, there are two possibilities:

::: card-list

- Don't make any assumptions about $\mu$
    - ❌ Cannot calculate probabilities 
    - $\rightarrow$ CIs
- Pretend that we know $\mu$
    - ✅ Can calculate probabilities
    - $\rightarrow$ p-values

:::
::::
:::::

# P-values

## 

::: card-list

- We will *pretend* to know $\mu$. What does this mean?
- This means that we can simulate what the sampling distribution would look like if we assume our *pretend* $\mu$ is true.
- What are good $\mu$'s to assume?

:::

## What $\mu$ to assume?

If we are interested in proving A, we cannot assume A.

::: card-list
- A circular argument: You cannot prove something if you already assume it is true.
- Examples of circular arguments:
    - I trust you because you are trustworthy
    - The scientific method works because science tells me so
    - Calibrating a compass by only using that one compass.
        - You need to use a second compass or known landmarks (like the stars).

:::

## A second compass 🧭🧭

::: card-list
- Choosing a $\mu$ is like choosing a second compass
- You need to make sure the pretend $\mu$ is different from the one you are actually interested in "proving".
- This is the purpose of a **null hypothesis**
    - The "opposite" hypothesis of your main hypothesis
:::

---

```{r}

area_between_norm(mu=0, sd=2, alpha=0.05, minlab=expression(mu-1.96 %*% SE), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(mu+1.96 %*% SE), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title=paste0(""))

```

Interpretation: given that the true mean is 0, the probability of getting a mean that is between $0 \pm 1.96 \times SE$ is 95%.


## {.center}

::: card-list

- Let's say in our experiment, we want to show that there is a difference between two groups. 
- The opposite hypothesis would be that there is no difference between the groups. AKA the difference = 0.
:::

---

We happen to observe the difference between two means (aka $\bar{x}_{observed}$) is $|1.96 \times SE|$

```{r}

area_between_norm(mu=0, sd=2, alpha=0.05, minlab=expression( -bar(x)[observed]), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(bar(x)[observed]), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title=paste0(""))

```

::: card-list
- Then the probability of getting a mean that is between $\pm\bar{x}_{observed}$ is __?
  - Answer: 95%
:::


##

```{r}

area_between_norm(mu=0, sd=2, alpha=0.05, minlab=expression( -bar(x)[observed]), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(bar(x)[observed]), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title=paste0(""))

```

But this is the opposite of the hypothesis we want to "prove". What would the opposite graph of this one look like?

---

```{r}

area_outside_norm <- function(mu, sd, alpha, minlab, meanlab, maxlab, xaxis, title){
percent <- paste0(as.character((1-alpha)*100),"%")

x <- seq(mu - 4*sd, mu + 4*sd, length.out = 1000)

df <- tibble(
  x = x,
  y = dnorm(x, mu, sd)
)

lower <- qnorm(alpha/2, mu, sd)
upper <- qnorm(1-(alpha/2), mu, sd)

mid_x <- (lower + upper) / 2
mid_y <- dnorm(mid_x, mu, sd) * 0.5

ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_area(
    aes(y = ifelse(x < lower | x > upper, y, 0)),
    alpha = 0.2,
    fill="steelblue"
  ) +
    labs(x = xaxis, title = title) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(lower, mu, upper), linetype = "dashed") + 
  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(-5,5), breaks = c(lower, mu, upper), labels = c(minlab,meanlab,maxlab)) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 10) + 
   theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = rel(1), face = "bold",
        hjust = 0.5,margin = margin(b = rel(4))),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y  = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.line.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.5),
    axis.ticks.x = element_line(linewidth = 0.8),
    axis.ticks.length.x = unit(4, "pt"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(1), margin = margin(t = rel(4))),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = rel(1.5), face = "bold", margin = margin(t = rel(3))),
    plot.margin = margin(b = rel(2), r = rel(2), l=rel(2), t=rel(2)),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
  plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "transparent")) +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = mid_x,
    y = mid_y,
    label = percent,
    size = 8
  )
}


plot4 <- area_outside_norm(mu=0, sd=1.5, alpha=0.1, minlab=expression(-bar(x)[observed]), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(bar(x)[observed]), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title="A")

plot5 <- area_outside_norm(mu=0, sd=1.5, alpha=0.2, minlab=expression(-bar(x)[observed]), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(bar(x)[observed]), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title=paste0("B"))

plot6 <- area_outside_norm(mu=0, sd=1.5, alpha=0.05, minlab=expression(mu-1.96 %*% SE), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(mu+1.96 %*% SE), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title=paste0("C"))

area_outside_norm(mu=0, sd=2, alpha=0.05, minlab=expression(-bar(x)[observed]), meanlab=expression(mu), maxlab=expression(bar(x)[observed]), xaxis=expression(bar(x)), title="")


```


Interpretation: given that the true mean is 0, the probability of sampling our observed $\bar{x}_{observed}$ (or something more extreme) is 100%-95% = 5%.

## Definition of p-value {.center}

::: card-list-center

- The p-value is the probability of observing our results (or something more extreme) given that our null hypothesis is true.

:::

---

The p-value probabilities depend on the actual observations (real data). Which of the following has the lowest p-value?

```{r}

plot4+plot5+plot6+theme(plot.margin = margin(b = 30, r = 30, l=30, t=30),)
```

::: card-list
- Answer: `A`. While `C` has the smallest area under the curve on the outside (5%), `C` is not plotting the actual observed means on the x-axis. `A` has the smallest area under the curve outside of the observed means (10%).

:::

# t-test

The t-test calculates the p-value for the difference between groups.

The function for conducting a t-test is `t.test()`. Use it like this:

```r
t.test(data = data, score ~ group)
```

And replace the names as needed.

# Deliverables

##

::: {.normal-list .nonincremental}

- [ ] Download [FlyingVsDrivingFearData.csv](/data/FlyingVsDrivingFearData.csv){.filelink}, and read the data into Rmd.
- [ ] Create a summary table for the dataset, grouping by `mode`.
- [ ] Simulate the sampling distribution, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. The null hypothesis is that the difference between driving and flying is 0.
    - [ ] Create an empty list named `sampling_dist`
    - [ ] Use a for loop for the following:
    - [ ] Simulate 1000 experiments
    - [ ] Simulate driving and flying data separately by using `rnorm()`. Use a sample size of 25, a mean of 0, and an sd of 1.
    - [ ] Take the difference between the mean of driving and the mean of flying, and add that to the `sampling_dist` list.
- [ ] Plot
    - [ ] Convert `sampling_dist` to a dataframe using `tibble()`
    - [ ] Plot a histogram and the simulated differences across experiments. Assign the plot to the variable `hist`
    - [ ] Calculate the observed difference between driving and flying from the actual dataset by using 

        ```r
        observed_diff <- sum_table$Mean[1] - sum_table$Mean[2]
        ```
    - [ ] Add the observed difference by using the following code:

        ```r
        hist + geom_vline(xintercept = -abs(observed_diff)) + geom_vline(xintercept = abs(observed_diff))
        ```
    - [ ] Run an official t-test (see previous page)
- [ ] Answer the following questions:
    - [ ] What does the final plot with the vertical lines show? 
    - [ ] If you had to guess the p-value based on the plot, what would you guess? 
    - [ ] How does your guess compare to the p-value from the t-test? Are they consistent?

:::

# What your deliverables might look like

---

:::: panel-tabset

## Raw data

```{r}

raw_data <- read_csv("./data/FlyingVsDrivingFearData.csv")
head(raw_data)

```

## Summary table

```{r}

sum_table <- raw_data %>% group_by(mode) %>% summarize(SampleSize=n(), Mean=mean(fear), SD=sd(fear))
sum_table
```

## Histogram

```{r}

sampling_dist <- c()

for (experiment in 1:1000){
    SampleSize=25
    driving <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=1)
    flying <- rnorm(n=SampleSize, mean=0, sd=1)
    sampling_dist[experiment] <- mean(driving) - mean(flying)

}

sim_df <- tibble(diffs=sampling_dist)

hist <- ggplot(sim_df, aes(x=diffs)) + geom_histogram()
hist
```

## Histogram with vertical lines

```{r}

observed_diff <- sum_table$Mean[1] - sum_table$Mean[2]
observed_diff

hist + geom_vline(xintercept = -abs(observed_diff)) + geom_vline(xintercept = abs(observed_diff))

```

```{r}

# Don't need this cell for students

sim_sum <- sim_df %>% mutate(greaterorless = 
    case_when(
        diffs > abs(observed_diff) ~ "greater", 
    diffs < -abs(observed_diff) ~ "less",
    TRUE ~ "between")
    ) %>% group_by(greaterorless) %>% summarize(count=n())

sim_sum

```

## t-test output
```{r}
t.test(data = raw_data, fear ~ mode)
```
